name: costly_feature_speaker
detail: ELPD-LOO -18729.2
hypothesis: Listeners reason about a speaker who balances communicative informativeness against an utterance production cost that penalizes more specific or discriminating features. This production cost makes the speaker less likely to name unique features, so listeners do not treat the mention of a shared feature as strong evidence against an object possessing an unmentioned unique feature.

name: naive_speaker_listener
detail: ELPD-LOO -18672.6
hypothesis: Listeners interpret utterances by directly inverting a naive production speaker who samples among the true features of the intended object, rather than mentalizing a recursive speaker who simulates listener comprehension. On asymmetric displays where a referent shares a feature with a distractor but possesses an unmentioned unique feature, this naive production model predicts equal choice between ambiguous referents because the speaker does not reason about alternative words. This sharply contrasts with standard pragmatic models, which infer that the speaker actively avoided the unique word and therefore penalize the uniquely identifiable referent.

name: costly_feature_speaker_2
detail: ELPD-LOO -18848.7
hypothesis: When choosing what to say about an object, speakers incur an utterance cost proportional to the number of objects sharing that feature in the visual context, reflecting a cognitive penalty for producing non-distinctive words beyond literal listener informativeness. The pragmatic listener inverts this cost-sensitive speaker, weakening scalar implicatures when alternative words are costly and expecting speakers to avoid shared labels when unique ones are available.

name: valence_salience_listener

Rather than assuming a deterministic mapping from features to words, the listener models the speaker as selecting a true descriptive feature of the intended referent, which is then mapped to an utterance through an uncertain lexical channel where alternative scene features have a non-zero probability of being named.

name: costly_feature_speaker
detail: elpd_diff 74.3 > 2.0 x clustered dse 16.1 vs softmax_belief_salience_listener
hypothesis: Listeners reason about a speaker who balances communicative informativeness against an utterance production cost that penalizes more specific or discriminating features. This production cost makes the speaker less likely to name unique features, so listeners do not treat the mention of a shared feature as strong evidence against an object possessing an unmentioned unique feature.

name: valence_salience_listener
detail: elpd_diff 89.6 > 2.0 x clustered dse 18.3 vs softmax_belief_salience_listener
hypothesis: Listeners assume that a speaker's communicative valence modulates object salience: feature complexity increases prior salience when referring to a favorite object, but this preference diminishes when referring to a least-favorite object. This valence-scaled salience prior is shared as common knowledge between speaker and listener in depth-1 pragmatic reasoning. Relative to rsa_l1_shared_prior, recursion depth remains at L1, one parameter w_valence is added to scale feature count by trial valence in the shared prior, and all other parameters and terms are retained unchanged.

name: rsa_l1_shared_prior
detail: elpd_diff 94.5 > 2.0 x clustered dse 20.9 vs softmax_belief_salience_listener
hypothesis: Depth-1 RSA with the salience prior as common knowledge, used by the simulated literal listener as well as the pragmatic listener.

name: rsa_l1_salience
detail: elpd_diff 94.8 > 2.0 x clustered dse 20.9 vs softmax_belief_salience_listener
hypothesis: Depth-1 RSA whose listener has a salience prior over objects (feature count, familiarization base rate) that the simulated literal listener lacks.

name: color_salience_shared_prior
detail: elpd_diff 95.1 > 2.0 x clustered dse 21.0 vs softmax_belief_salience_listener
hypothesis: Listeners incorporate visual color contrast into object salience, expecting speakers to refer to full-color objects over grayscale ones. This color-salience preference is shared as common knowledge between speaker and listener in depth-1 pragmatic reasoning. Relative to rsa_l1_shared_prior, recursion depth remains unchanged at L1, one parameter w_color is added to the salience prior with a Normal(0, 1) prior, no parameters are removed, and the color salience weight multiplies the color indicator (1 minus grayscale) in the shared prior logits.

name: aspect_qud_listener
detail: elpd_diff 133.8 > 2.0 x clustered dse 20.7 vs softmax_belief_salience_listener
hypothesis: Listeners interpret referring expressions by modeling a speaker whose communicative goal addresses a specific aspect or property of the referent rather than its full identity. For an intended referent, the speaker selects an aspect from among the referent's true features and chooses an utterance to informatively communicate that aspect to a literal listener. The pragmatic listener jointly reasons about the speaker's intended referent and latent communicative goal, selecting referents by marginalizing over the question under discussion.

name: costly_feature_speaker_2
detail: elpd_diff 193.8 > 2.0 x clustered dse 26.5 vs softmax_belief_salience_listener
hypothesis: When choosing what to say about an object, speakers incur an utterance cost proportional to the number of objects sharing that feature in the visual context, reflecting a cognitive penalty for producing non-distinctive words beyond literal listener informativeness. The pragmatic listener inverts this cost-sensitive speaker, weakening scalar implicatures when alternative words are costly and expecting speakers to avoid shared labels when unique ones are available.

name: rsa_l1
detail: elpd_diff 406.9 > 2.0 x clustered dse 73.4 vs softmax_belief_salience_listener
hypothesis: Listeners invert a softmax-rational speaker who simulates a literal listener (depth 1), with a uniform prior over objects.

name: rsa_l2
detail: elpd_diff 407.2 > 2.0 x clustered dse 73.4 vs softmax_belief_salience_listener
hypothesis: Listeners reason one level deeper (depth 2), inverting a speaker who simulates the depth-1 pragmatic listener.

name: associative_resonance_listener
detail: retired by the cap of 8 live models
hypothesis: Listeners interpret referring expressions through bi-directional associative resonance between the heard word and candidate objects in the scene. Upon hearing an utterance, referent selection is driven by the joint resonance of forward cue validity—how specifically the word singles out an object across the display—and backward category validity—how strongly the object evokes that word among its own features. Candidate objects with high bi-directional resonance are selected, while attentional lapses default to bottom-up perceptual salience.

name: fewest_features_listener
detail: retired by the cap of 8 live models
hypothesis: Listeners interpret referring expressions using a non-Bayesian parsimony heuristic rather than recursive speaker mentalization: upon hearing a word, they identify candidate objects of which the word is literally true and choose the candidate possessing the fewest total features. By penalizing objects with extraneous unmentioned features, listeners resolve referential ambiguity without computing alternative speaker utterances or Bayesian likelihoods.
